newsitem.title: USA: U.S. surprised at remarks by Croatia's Tudjman.
newsitem.headline: U.S. surprised at remarks by Croatia's Tudjman.

text.p: The United States said on Monday it was surprised at anti-U.S. remarks by Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, long a key U.S. ally in the volatile Balkans.
"We were surprised by the tone of President Tudjman's speech earlier this month at a party conference in Zagreb," acting State Department spokesman Glyn Davies told reporters.

"Suggestions that Croatia is moving away from the U.S. and the West are inconsistent with what we have heard in the past and do not reflect the direction we hope to move in our bilateral relations," he said.

Tudjman, apparently angered by U.S. efforts to promote democratic reforms in his country, has acccused the U.S. Embassy in Zagreb of encouraging opponents intent on unseating him and the Croatian Democratic Union in elections scheduled for next year.
Without providing details, he said he felt compelled to take action "more openly" against U.S. Ambassador Peter Galbraith, who has increasingly championed a human rights agenda.

Davies praised Galbraith as serving "with distincition" and said the ambassador had acted appropriately in carrying out his instructions. "He has obviously the confidence of both the president and the secretary of state," Davies added.

In a possible reflection of his anger at the United States, Tudjman reportedly blocked a $400 million sale of Boeing Co. aircraft to Croatian Airlines in recent weeks. The airlines now reportedly plans to buy six aircraft from the European consortium Airbus Industrie instead.

"The U.S. government strongly supported Boeing's bid to provide aircraft to Croatia," Davies said when asked about the sale. "The Croatian government has denied that political concerns played a role in their decision not to buy from Boeing."

Although the United States and Croatia shared many common interests and had worked together effectively on the peace process in Bosnia, he said, "we do have areas of concern which we have made clear to the Croatian government at the highest levels."

Among these were restrictions on the media such as the crackdown on Radio 101, a Zagreb station that the authorities announced would be stripped of its license on the ground it was "too politicized," the State Department spokesman said.
